claim: Unipolar brush cells (UBCs) are enriched in cerebellar areas that control balance and eye movement.
source: Unipolar brush cells (UBCs), and Purkinje cell (PC) synapses made by axon collaterals in the granular layer, are both enriched in areas that control balance and eye movement.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about the regional distribution of UBCs.

claim: Purkinje cell synapses made by axon collaterals in the granular layer are enriched in areas that control balance and eye movement.
source: Unipolar brush cells (UBCs), and Purkinje cell (PC) synapses made by axon collaterals in the granular layer, are both enriched in areas that control balance and eye movement.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about the regional distribution of PC synapses.

claim: Purkinje cells preferentially inhibit metabotropic glutamate receptor type 1 (mGluR1)-expressing UBCs.
source: Here, we find a link between these specializations in mice: PCs preferentially inhibit metabotropic glutamate receptor type 1 (mGluR1)-expressing UBCs that respond to mossy fiber (MF) inputs with long lasting increases in firing, but PCs do not inhibit mGluR1-lacking UBCs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: mGluR1-expressing UBCs respond to mossy fiber inputs with long lasting increases in firing.
source: PCs preferentially inhibit metabotropic glutamate receptor type 1 (mGluR1)-expressing UBCs that respond to mossy fiber (MF) inputs with long lasting increases in firing
evidence: This characterizes the functional properties of mGluR1-expressing UBCs and is supported by prior literature and data in this study.

claim: Purkinje cells do not inhibit mGluR1-lacking UBCs.
source: PCs preferentially inhibit metabotropic glutamate receptor type 1 (mGluR1)-expressing UBCs that respond to mossy fiber (MF) inputs with long lasting increases in firing, but PCs do not inhibit mGluR1-lacking UBCs.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing no PC inhibition in mGluR1-negative cells.

claim: Purkinje cells inhibit about 29% of mGluR1-expressing UBCs by activating GABAA receptors.
source: PCs inhibit about 29% of mGluR1-expressing UBCs by activating GABAA receptors (GABAARs) and inhibit almost all mGluR1-expressing UBCs by activating GABAB receptors (GABABRs).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: Purkinje cells inhibit almost all mGluR1-expressing UBCs by activating GABAB receptors.
source: PCs inhibit about 29% of mGluR1-expressing UBCs by activating GABAA receptors (GABAARs) and inhibit almost all mGluR1-expressing UBCs by activating GABAB receptors (GABABRs).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: GABAAR-mediated feedback from PCs to UBCs is fast and unreliable.
source: Based on optogenetic studies and a small number of paired recordings, GABAAR-mediated feedback is fast and unreliable.
evidence: This characterization is based on experimental data from optogenetic studies and paired recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: GABABR-mediated inhibition from PCs to UBCs is slower than GABAAR-mediated inhibition.
source: GABABR-mediated inhibition is slower and is sufficiently large to strongly influence the input-output transformations of mGluR1-expressing UBCs.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements of the kinetics of GABABR-mediated currents.

claim: GABABR-mediated inhibition is sufficiently large to strongly influence the input-output transformations of mGluR1-expressing UBCs.
source: GABABR-mediated inhibition is slower and is sufficiently large to strongly influence the input-output transformations of mGluR1-expressing UBCs.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing the magnitude of GABABR-mediated currents and their effects on UBC firing.

claim: Different lobules of the cerebellar cortex are engaged in diverse motor and non-motor behaviors.
source: Although different lobules of the cerebellar cortex are engaged in diverse motor and non-motor behaviors (Ito, 1998; Kim and Thompson, 1997; Massion, 1992; Murdoch, 2010; Schmahmann and Sherman, 1998; Siuda et al., 2014; Van Overwalle et al., 2014; Villanueva, 2012), a basic circuit motif is repeated within each functional compartment.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: A basic circuit motif is repeated within each functional compartment of the cerebellar cortex.
source: Although different lobules of the cerebellar cortex are engaged in diverse motor and non-motor behaviors (Ito, 1998; Kim and Thompson, 1997; Massion, 1992; Murdoch, 2010; Schmahmann and Sherman, 1998; Siuda et al., 2014; Van Overwalle et al., 2014; Villanueva, 2012), a basic circuit motif is repeated within each functional compartment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar organization.

claim: Mossy fibers provide excitatory inputs to granule cells.
source: Mossy fibers provide excitatory inputs to granule cells (GrCs) (Delvendahl and Hallermann, 2016; DiGregorio et al., 2002; Huang et al., 2013; Sotelo, 2008)
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar circuitry supported by multiple citations.

claim: Granule cells excite Purkinje cells.
source: Mossy fibers provide excitatory inputs to granule cells (GrCs) (Delvendahl and Hallermann, 2016; DiGregorio et al., 2002; Huang et al., 2013; Sotelo, 2008), which in turn excite Purkinje cells (PCs) that provide the output of the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar circuitry.

claim: Purkinje cells provide the output of the cerebellar cortex.
source: Mossy fibers provide excitatory inputs to granule cells (GrCs) (Delvendahl and Hallermann, 2016; DiGregorio et al., 2002; Huang et al., 2013; Sotelo, 2008), which in turn excite Purkinje cells (PCs) that provide the output of the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar circuitry.

claim: Golgi cells inhibit granule cells.
source: In addition, Golgi cells (GoCs) inhibit GrCs, and molecular layer interneurons inhibit PCs (Eccles, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar circuitry supported by citation.

claim: Molecular layer interneurons inhibit Purkinje cells.
source: In addition, Golgi cells (GoCs) inhibit GrCs, and molecular layer interneurons inhibit PCs (Eccles, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar circuitry supported by citation.

claim: Regional synaptic and cellular specializations exist beyond the basic circuit motif of the cerebellar cortex.
source: Regional synaptic and cellular specializations exist beyond this basic circuit motif, presumably to meet the computational demands associated with specific behaviors (Cerminara et al., 2015; Diño et al., 1999; Guo et al., 2016; Kozareva et al., 2021; Sekerková et al., 2014; Suvrathan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Regional specializations in the cerebellar cortex presumably meet the computational demands associated with specific behaviors.
source: Regional synaptic and cellular specializations exist beyond this basic circuit motif, presumably to meet the computational demands associated with specific behaviors (Cerminara et al., 2015; Diño et al., 1999; Guo et al., 2016; Kozareva et al., 2021; Sekerková et al., 2014; Suvrathan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of regional specializations.

claim: The density of unipolar brush cells exhibits large regional variation.
source: One of the most obvious specializations is that the density of unipolar brush cells (UBCs) exhibits large regional variation (Diño et al., 1999; Sekerková et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: UBCs are excitatory interneurons located in the granular layer.
source: UBCs are excitatory interneurons located in the granular layer that are usually innervated by a single MF (Mugnaini and Floris, 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge about UBC identity and location, supported by citation.

claim: UBCs are usually innervated by a single mossy fiber.
source: UBCs are excitatory interneurons located in the granular layer that are usually innervated by a single MF (Mugnaini and Floris, 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge about UBC connectivity, supported by citation.

claim: UBCs contribute to temporal processing by converting short-lived mossy fiber signals into long-lasting changes in UBC activity.
source: UBCs contribute to temporal processing by converting short-lived MF signals into long-lasting changes in UBC activity (Kennedy et al., 2014; Kinney et al., 1997; Kreko-Pierce et al., 2020; Locatelli et al., 2013; Mugnaini and Floris, 1994; Mugnaini et al., 2011; Rossi et al., 1995; van Dorp and De Zeeuw, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Mossy fibers excite UBCs that express metabotropic glutamate receptor type 1 (mGluR1).
source: MFs excite UBCs that express metabotropic glutamate receptor type I (mGluR1), suppress firing in UBCs where mGluR2 is prominent, and evoke more complex responses in other UBCs that express both mGluR1 and mGluR2 (Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015; Guo et al., 2021; Kinney et al., 1997; Knoflach and Kemp, 1998; Rossi et al., 1995; Russo et al., 2008; van Dorp and De Zeeuw, 2014; Zampini et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Mossy fibers suppress firing in UBCs where mGluR2 is prominent.
source: MFs excite UBCs that express metabotropic glutamate receptor type I (mGluR1), suppress firing in UBCs where mGluR2 is prominent, and evoke more complex responses in other UBCs that express both mGluR1 and mGluR2 (Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015; Guo et al., 2021; Kinney et al., 1997; Knoflach and Kemp, 1998; Rossi et al., 1995; Russo et al., 2008; van Dorp and De Zeeuw, 2014; Zampini et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Mossy fibers evoke complex responses in UBCs that express both mGluR1 and mGluR2.
source: MFs excite UBCs that express metabotropic glutamate receptor type I (mGluR1), suppress firing in UBCs where mGluR2 is prominent, and evoke more complex responses in other UBCs that express both mGluR1 and mGluR2 (Borges-Merjane and Trussell, 2015; Guo et al., 2021; Kinney et al., 1997; Knoflach and Kemp, 1998; Rossi et al., 1995; Russo et al., 2008; van Dorp and De Zeeuw, 2014; Zampini et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: UBCs are often disregarded in descriptions of the circuitry of the cerebellar cortex.
source: UBCs are often disregarded in descriptions of the circuitry of the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical treatment of UBCs in the literature.

claim: UBCs are present in all areas of the cerebellar cortex.
source: However, UBCs are present in all areas and are exceptionally dense in some regions, notably those involved in vestibular function (Diño et al., 1999; Takács et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: UBCs are exceptionally dense in regions involved in vestibular function.
source: However, UBCs are present in all areas and are exceptionally dense in some regions, notably those involved in vestibular function (Diño et al., 1999; Takács et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: UBCs are more prevalent and widely distributed in larger mammals including humans.
source: UBCs are more prevalent and widely distributed in larger mammals including humans (Diño et al., 1999; Munoz, 1990), suggesting a special role in the complex cerebellar computations relating to higher cognition.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The prevalence of UBCs in larger mammals suggests a special role in complex cerebellar computations relating to higher cognition.
source: UBCs are more prevalent and widely distributed in larger mammals including humans (Diño et al., 1999; Munoz, 1990), suggesting a special role in the complex cerebellar computations relating to higher cognition.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of UBC distribution.

claim: Purkinje cell feedback via collaterals is restricted to parasagittal planes.
source: PC feedback via collaterals that are restricted to parasagittal planes is another noteworthy regional specialization (Witter et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Each Purkinje cell axon has a collateral that inhibits Purkinje cells.
source: In addition to sending an axon to the deep cerebellar nuclei, each PC axon has a collateral that inhibits PCs (Bernard and Axelrad, 1993; Bernard et al., 1993; Bornschein et al., 2013; de Solages et al., 2008; Orduz and Llano, 2007; Watt et al., 2009; Witter et al., 2016) and several types of inhibitory interneurons in the cerebellar cortex (Crook et al., 2007; Hirono et al., 2012; Witter et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Purkinje cell axon collaterals inhibit several types of inhibitory interneurons in the cerebellar cortex.
source: In addition to sending an axon to the deep cerebellar nuclei, each PC axon has a collateral that inhibits PCs (Bernard and Axelrad, 1993; Bernard et al., 1993; Bornschein et al., 2013; de Solages et al., 2008; Orduz and Llano, 2007; Watt et al., 2009; Witter et al., 2016) and several types of inhibitory interneurons in the cerebellar cortex (Crook et al., 2007; Hirono et al., 2012; Witter et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: In some regions, Purkinje cells make extensive contacts within the granular layer and inhibit granule cells.
source: In some regions, PCs make extensive contacts within the granular layer and inhibit GrCs (Guo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: PC to granule cell feedback is mediated primarily by GABAA receptors.
source: This feedback is mediated primarily by GABAA receptors (GABAARs) and has a prominent slow component that suggests the involvement of the extrasynaptic high-affinity GABAARs.
evidence: This is based on prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: PC to granule cell feedback has a prominent slow component that suggests the involvement of extrasynaptic high-affinity GABAARs.
source: This feedback is mediated primarily by GABAA receptors (GABAARs) and has a prominent slow component that suggests the involvement of the extrasynaptic high-affinity GABAARs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetics of the response.

claim: PC to granule cell synapses allow the output of the cerebellar cortex to provide slow negative feedback to inhibit the input layer.
source: These PC to GrC synapses allow the output of the cerebellar cortex to provide slow negative feedback to inhibit the input layer.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional role of PC to GrC synapses.

claim: PC to granule cell synapses are most prominent in regions involved in vestibular function.
source: Like UBCs, these synapses are also most prominent in regions involved in vestibular function.
evidence: This is based on prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: The regional overlap of high densities of UBCs and granular layer PC synapses raises the possibility that PCs might inhibit UBCs.
source: The regional overlap of high densities of UBCs and granular layer PC synapses raises the possibility that PCs might inhibit UBCs and thereby allow PC feedback to refine temporal processing.
evidence: This is the hypothesis that motivated the study.

claim: PC inhibition of UBCs could allow PC feedback to refine temporal processing.
source: The regional overlap of high densities of UBCs and granular layer PC synapses raises the possibility that PCs might inhibit UBCs and thereby allow PC feedback to refine temporal processing.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the functional significance of PC to UBC connections.

claim: Purkinje cells phasically inhibit a subset of UBCs by activating GABAARs.
source: We find that PCs phasically inhibit a subset of UBCs by activating GABAARs, and that UBCs with prominent mGluR1 signaling are preferentially targeted.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: UBCs with prominent mGluR1 signaling are preferentially targeted by PC inhibition.
source: We find that PCs phasically inhibit a subset of UBCs by activating GABAARs, and that UBCs with prominent mGluR1 signaling are preferentially targeted.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Purkinje cells provide long-lasting inhibition to most mGluR1-expressing UBCs by activating GABAB receptors.
source: PCs also provide long-lasting inhibition to most mGluR1-expressing UBCs by activating GABAB receptors (GABABRs).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: PC inhibition of mGluR1-expressing UBCs provides direct feedback from the output layer to input layer to influence the first stage of cerebellar processing.
source: In these ways, PC inhibition of mGluR1-expressing UBCs provides direct feedback from the output layer to input layer to influence the first stage of cerebellar processing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: The highest densities of both UBCs and granular layer PC synapses were found in vestibular regions (lobules IX, X, FL, and PFL).
source: The highest densities of both UBCs and granular layer PC synapses were found in vestibular regions (lobules IX, X, FL, and PFL; see Figure 1C, D and F-I) and in the oculomotor vermis (lobules VIb and VII, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of confocal images shown in Figure 1.

claim: High densities of both UBCs and granular layer PC synapses were found in the oculomotor vermis (lobules VIb and VII).
source: The highest densities of both UBCs and granular layer PC synapses were found in vestibular regions (lobules IX, X, FL, and PFL; see Figure 1C, D and F-I) and in the oculomotor vermis (lobules VIb and VII, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of confocal images shown in Figure 1.

claim: Much lower densities of UBCs and PC synapses were observed in the anterior cerebellar cortex (lobules I–V and VIa) and lobule VIII.
source: Much lower densities were observed in the anterior cerebellar cortex (lobules I–V and VIa; see Figure 1C,E) and lobule VIII.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of confocal images shown in Figure 1.

claim: In lobule X, there was a particularly high density of PC collateral synapses and UBCs.
source: In lobule X, there was a particularly high density of PC collateral synapses and UBCs (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of confocal images shown in Figure 1J.

claim: High-power images of lobule X suggest that PC synapses directly terminate on the brushes and the cell bodies of many UBCs.
source: High-power images of lobule X suggest that PC synapses directly terminate on the brushes and the cell bodies of many UBCs (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is based on visual inspection of high-resolution confocal images shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Electrophysiological studies have shown that fast inhibition in UBCs is mediated by a combination of glycine and GABAARs.
source: Electrophysiological studies have shown that fast inhibition in UBCs is mediated by a combination of glycine and GABAARs (Dugué et al., 2005; Rousseau et al., 2012), but that mGluR1-lacking UBCs lack GABAARs (Rousseau et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: mGluR1-lacking UBCs lack GABAARs.
source: Electrophysiological studies have shown that fast inhibition in UBCs is mediated by a combination of glycine and GABAARs (Dugué et al., 2005; Rousseau et al., 2012), but that mGluR1-lacking UBCs lack GABAARs (Rousseau et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: α1, β2, β3, and γ2 subunits of GABAARs have a gradient of expression levels and are selectively enriched in mGluR1-positive UBCs.
source: Consistent with these observations, molecular profiling of UBCs using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNASeq) (Kozareva et al., 2021) indicate that α1, β2, β3, and γ2 subunits of GABAARs have a gradient of expression levels and are selectively enriched in mGluR1-positive UBCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), but that glycine receptors are broadly expressed by UBCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Glycine receptors are broadly expressed by UBCs.
source: Consistent with these observations, molecular profiling of UBCs using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNASeq) (Kozareva et al., 2021) indicate that α1, β2, β3, and γ2 subunits of GABAARs have a gradient of expression levels and are selectively enriched in mGluR1-positive UBCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), but that glycine receptors are broadly expressed by UBCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The molecular identity of UBCs could determine whether they receive PC feedback.
source: This opens the possibility that the molecular identity of UBCs could determine whether they receive PC feedback.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the differential expression of GABAAR subunits.

claim: Optical stimulation evoked currents in 17 out of 41 UBCs tested.
source: Optical stimulation evoked currents in a subpopulation of these cells (Figure 2B right, Figure 2D asterisk marks, 17/41 cells) but not in others (Figure 2C, right, 24/41 cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: GABAAR antagonist gabazine eliminated light-evoked synaptic currents in UBCs.
source: GABAAR antagonist gabazine eliminated these light-evoked synaptic currents (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2E demonstrating pharmacological blockade.

claim: PC GABAA feedback preferentially targets UBCs that are excited by glutamatergic inputs.
source: Cumulative histograms for glutamate-evoked charge transfer (Figure 2F), and the average glutamate-evoked current for UBCs with or without PC feedback (Figure 2G), show that PC GABAA feedback preferentially targets UBCs that are excited by glutamatergic inputs.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the data shown in Figure 2F and 2G.

claim: DHPG puffs evoked spiking in 45 out of 60 UBCs tested.
source: DHPG (100mM, 50 ms) puffs evoked spiking in a subset of UBCs (Figure 2I,J, left, K 45/60).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DHPG application experiments shown in Figure 2K.

claim: 13 out of 45 DHPG-responsive UBCs had significant light-evoked responses.
source: After recording the DHPG-evoked increase in firing with a cell-attached electrode, we obtained a whole-cell configuration and measured light-evoked responses. 13/45 DHPG-responsive UBCs also had significant light-evoked responses (Figure 2I,J, right, K).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the combined DHPG and optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 2K.

claim: PC GABAAR-mediated feedback preferentially targets UBCs with larger mGluR1-mediated excitation.
source: Cumulative histograms for DHPG-evoked firing rate increases in UBCs (Figure 2L), and the average DHPG-evoked firing rate increases for UBCs with or without PC feedback (Figure 2M), show that PC GABAAR-mediated feedback preferentially targets UBCs with larger mGluR1-mediated excitation.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the data shown in Figure 2L and 2M.

claim: There is considerable scatter in the amplitudes of the average GABAA responses evoked by optical stimulation.
source: There is considerable scatter in the amplitudes of the average GABAA responses evoked by optical stimulation (Figure 2N).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 2N.

claim: The IPSC latency in PC to UBC paired recordings was 1.5±0.4 ms.
source: The IPSC latency was 1.5±0.4 ms (Figure 3C,D,F) and the distribution of response amplitude was approximately Gaussian (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from paired recordings shown in Figure 3.

claim: The distribution of PC to UBC response amplitude was approximately Gaussian.
source: The IPSC latency was 1.5±0.4 ms (Figure 3C,D,F) and the distribution of response amplitude was approximately Gaussian (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The response potency of PC to UBC synapses is large.
source: While the response potency is large (Figure 3F), there was a high failure rate of approximately 85% (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from paired recordings shown in Figure 3F.

claim: PC to UBC synapses have a high failure rate of approximately 85%.
source: While the response potency is large (Figure 3F), there was a high failure rate of approximately 85% (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from paired recordings shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Only mGluR1-positive UBCs contain GABABRs.
source: Previous studies established that only mGluR1-positive UBCs contain GABABRs (Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: GABABRs comprise GB1 and GB2 subunits.
source: GABABRs comprises GB1 and GB2 subunits (Gassmann and Bettler, 2012) that are encoded by Gabbr1 and Gabbr2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GABABR structure supported by citation.

claim: UBCs exhibit a gradient of expression of Gabbr2 that is similar to Grm1 (mGluR1).
source: UBCs exhibit a gradient of expression of Gabbr2 that is similar to Grm1 (mGluR1), and Gabbr1 has a less pronounced gradient of expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Gabbr1 has a less pronounced gradient of expression in UBCs than Gabbr2.
source: UBCs exhibit a gradient of expression of Gabbr2 that is similar to Grm1 (mGluR1), and Gabbr1 has a less pronounced gradient of expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: GABABRs are heterodimers consisting of GABAB1 and GABAB2 receptors.
source: The differences in the expression patterns of Gabbr2 and Gabbr1 are intriguing, because it is thought that GABABRs are heterodimers consisting of GABAB1 and GABAB2 receptors (Frangaj and Fan, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about GABABR structure supported by citation.

claim: In whole-cell recordings, the currents evoked by GABABR agonists washed out within minutes.
source: We found that in whole-cell recordings the currents evoked by GABABR agonists washed out within minutes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B, gray).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Washout of GABABR responses in whole-cell recordings was accompanied by an increase in the leak current.
source: This washout was accompanied by an increase in the leak current (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In perforated patch recordings, GABAB responses were large and stable.
source: In contrast, in perforated patch recordings, GABAB responses were large and stable, and leak currents were also stable (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, black).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Perforated patch recordings facilitate the measurement of PC-evoked GABAB responses.
source: These experiments established that perforated patch recordings facilitate the measurement of PC-evoked GABAB responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of whole-cell and perforated patch recordings.

claim: Optical stimulation evoked outward currents in all 13 UBCs tested for GABABR responses.
source: Optical stimulation evoked outward currents in all UBCs (Figure 4E–G, 13/13).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: GABABR-mediated inhibition in UBCs is slow with a rise time constant of 583±6 ms and decay time constant of 533±5 ms.
source: GABABR-mediated inhibition was slow (Figure 4F, rise time constant=583±6 ms, decay time constant=533±5 ms).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of the kinetics shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The GABABR antagonist CGP eliminated light-evoked responses in UBCs.
source: The GABABR antagonist CGP eliminated these light-evoked responses (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4K demonstrating pharmacological blockade.

claim: The average GABABR-mediated inhibition of 3.8±2.2 pA was sufficiently large to strongly suppress or entirely shut down spontaneous UBC firing in 9 out of 10 spontaneously firing UBCs.
source: The average inhibition of 3.8±2.2 pA was sufficiently large to strongly suppress or entirely shut down spontaneous UBC firing (Figure 4H–J in 9/10 spontaneous firing UBCs).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments shown in Figure 4H-J.

claim: PC firing rates dynamically regulate the activation of GABABRs on UBCs.
source: These findings suggest that PC firing rates dynamically regulate the activation of GABABRs, and by extension the spontaneous firing of most mGluR1+ UBCs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: PC firing rates dynamically regulate the spontaneous firing of most mGluR1+ UBCs.
source: These findings suggest that PC firing rates dynamically regulate the activation of GABABRs, and by extension the spontaneous firing of most mGluR1+ UBCs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: With GABABR-dependent mechanism, PCs inhibit 90-100% of mGluR1+ UBCs (13/13 DHPG responding cells and 9/10 spontaneous firing).
source: With this GABABR-dependent mechanism, PCs inhibit a much larger fraction of mGluR1+ UBCs (90–100%, Figure 4G, 13/13 DHPG responding cells and Figure 4J, 9/10 spontaneous firing), compared to GABAAR-dependent inhibition (29%, Figure 2K, 13/45 DHPG-responding cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of the prevalence of GABABR vs GABAAR-mediated inhibition.

claim: GABAAR-dependent inhibition by PCs affects 29% of mGluR1+ UBCs (13/45 DHPG-responding cells).
source: With this GABABR-dependent mechanism, PCs inhibit a much larger fraction of mGluR1+ UBCs (90–100%, Figure 4G, 13/13 DHPG responding cells and Figure 4J, 9/10 spontaneous firing), compared to GABAAR-dependent inhibition (29%, Figure 2K, 13/45 DHPG-responding cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Slow PC-UBC inhibition represents the average synaptic contribution from multiple PCs.
source: Slow PC-UBC inhibition represents the average synaptic contribution from multiple PCs, and when the firing rates of these PCs are elevated UBCs are hyperpolarized.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mechanism underlying slow inhibition.

claim: When the firing rates of PCs are elevated, UBCs are hyperpolarized.
source: Slow PC-UBC inhibition represents the average synaptic contribution from multiple PCs, and when the firing rates of these PCs are elevated UBCs are hyperpolarized.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing GABABR-mediated hyperpolarization.

claim: Hyperpolarization can relieve the inactivation of T-type calcium channels and make neurons burst upon depolarization.
source: As has been shown previously, hyperpolarization can relieve the inactivation of T-type calcium channels and make neurons burst upon depolarization (Perez-Reyes, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge about T-type calcium channels supported by citation.

claim: A 5-pA tonic hyperpolarizing current drastically altered UBC responses to current steps, with current steps evoking a much larger transient response and reduced steady-state firing.
source: A 5-pA tonic hyperpolarizing current, drastically altered these responses, with current steps evoking a much larger transient response and reduced steady-state firing (Figure 5A,B and C, black right).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: In all cells tested, hyperpolarization increased the difference between peak and steady-state firing rates.
source: In all cells, hyperpolarization increased the difference between peak and steady-state firing rates (Figure 5C, n=4).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Full-field optical excitation of PCs activated GABABR-mediated inhibition and produced qualitatively similar effects on spiking as hyperpolarizing current injections.
source: Full-field optical excitation of PCs activated GABABR-mediated inhibition and produced qualitatively similar effects on spiking as hyperpolarizing current injections (Figure 5D, blue, right).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Optical activation of PC feedback through GABABR hyperpolarized UBCs.
source: Optical activation of PC feedback through GABABR hyperpolarized UBCs (Figure 5D, blue, right), and current steps evoked larger initial responses and smaller steady-state responses (Figure 5E,F, blue vs. gray).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: With PC feedback, current steps evoked larger initial responses and smaller steady-state responses in UBCs.
source: Optical activation of PC feedback through GABABR hyperpolarized UBCs (Figure 5D, blue, right), and current steps evoked larger initial responses and smaller steady-state responses (Figure 5E,F, blue vs. gray).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: The effects of PC inhibition of UBCs may be more complex than simply suppressing spiking in UBCs.
source: These counterintuitive effects on spiking, in which a hyperpolarization increases initial responses, are consistent with previously described properties of UBCs (Perez-Reyes, 2003). They suggest that the effects of PC inhibition of UBCs may be more complex than simply suppressing spiking in UBCs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Brief application of baclofen following DHPG reduced the number of evoked spikes in UBCs.
source: Brief application of baclofen following DHPG reduced the number of evoked spikes (Figure 5H–J).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5H-J.

claim: Activation of GABABRs can strongly suppress mGluR1-activated UBC firing.
source: Thus, activation of GABABRs, as could occur when PC activity is elevated, can strongly suppress mGluR1-activated UBC firing (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data with DHPG and baclofen.

claim: PC to UBC synapses link two previously described regional specializations of the cerebellar cortex: the high densities of UBCs and the prevalence of PC synapses within the granular layer.
source: The PC to UBC synapses described here link two previously described regional specializations of the cerebellar cortex: the high densities of UBCs and the prevalence of PC synapses within the granular layer.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding.

claim: PC to UBC synapses provide a new way for PC outputs to dynamically regulate the temporal transformations by UBC populations within the input layer.
source: PC to UBC synapses provide a new way for PC outputs to dynamically regulate the temporal transformations by UBC populations within the input layer.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Optical stimulation of PC terminals evoked GABAAR-mediated responses in 29% (30/101) of UBCs.
source: Optical stimulation of PC terminals evoked GABAAR-mediated responses in 29% (30/101) of UBCs.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the optogenetic experiments.

claim: Light-evoked PC GABAAR-mediated inhibition was observed in three cases where glutamate evoked inhibitory currents.
source: Light-evoked PC GABAAR-mediated inhibition was much more common in cells in which glutamate evoked a large excitatory current but was also observed in three cases where glutamate evoked inhibitory currents (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A large mGluR2 component could obscure a small mGluR1 component in some UBCs.
source: This may reflect the graded nature of metabotropic glutamate receptor signaling in UBCs in which outward mGluR1-mediated currents and inward mGluR2-mediated currents can be present in the same cell, and a large mGluR2 component could obscure a small mGluR1 component in some cells (Guo et al., 2021; Kozareva et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation to explain the observation of PC inhibition in some cells with inhibitory glutamate responses.

claim: PCs did not inhibit any mGluR1− UBCs (0/15).
source: When we used DHPG to identify mGluR1+ cells, we found that PCs did not inhibit any mGluR1− UBCs (0/15), (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments shown in Figure 2K.

claim: mGluR1− UBCs do not respond to either GABAAR or GABABR agonists.
source: This is in keeping with the observations that mGluR1− UBCs do not respond to either GABAAR or GABABR agonists (Kim et al., 2012; Rousseau et al., 2012), that they do not express GABAAR or GABABR subunits (Rousseau et al., 2012; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and that PCs do not release glycine (Tanaka and Ezure, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: mGluR1− UBCs do not express GABAAR or GABABR subunits.
source: This is in keeping with the observations that mGluR1− UBCs do not respond to either GABAAR or GABABR agonists (Kim et al., 2012; Rousseau et al., 2012), that they do not express GABAAR or GABABR subunits (Rousseau et al., 2012; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and that PCs do not release glycine (Tanaka and Ezure, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: PCs do not release glycine.
source: This is in keeping with the observations that mGluR1− UBCs do not respond to either GABAAR or GABABR agonists (Kim et al., 2012; Rousseau et al., 2012), that they do not express GABAAR or GABABR subunits (Rousseau et al., 2012; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and that PCs do not release glycine (Tanaka and Ezure, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Glycinergic Golgi cells can inhibit all UBCs.
source: In contrast to PCs that only inhibit a subset of UBCs, glycinergic GoCs can inhibit all UBCs, because ionotropic glycine receptors and glycinergic IPSCs are present in all UBCs (Dugué et al., 2005; Rousseau et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ionotropic glycine receptors and glycinergic IPSCs are present in all UBCs.
source: In contrast to PCs that only inhibit a subset of UBCs, glycinergic GoCs can inhibit all UBCs, because ionotropic glycine receptors and glycinergic IPSCs are present in all UBCs (Dugué et al., 2005; Rousseau et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Approximately 50% of inhibitory synapses onto UBCs co-release GABA and glycine and the rest only release GABA.
source: Our findings provide new insights into the previous immunohistochemical characterization of the inhibitory synapses onto UBCs that suggested approximately 50% co-release GABA and glycine and the rest only release GABA (Dugué et al., 2005; Rousseau et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on prior immunohistochemical studies cited.

claim: It was previously thought that exclusively GABAergic synapses onto UBCs were made by non-glycinergic Golgi cells.
source: Previously it was thought that these exclusively GABAergic synapses were made by non-glycinergic GoCs.
evidence: This describes a previous interpretation in the literature.

claim: PCs likely constitute most of the exclusively GABAergic synapses onto UBCs.
source: Our findings suggest that PCs likely constitute most of these synapses.
evidence: This is a new interpretation based on the findings of this study.

claim: Light-evoked GABAB currents are observed in a larger percentage of mGluR1+ UBCs (>90%) than are light-evoked GABAA currents (29%).
source: PCs inhibit UBCs by activating both GABAARs and GABABRs, and light-evoked GABAB currents are observed in a larger percentage of mGluR1+ UBCs (>90%) than are light-evoked GABAA currents (29%).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of the prevalence of GABABR vs GABAAR-mediated responses.

claim: The difference in prevalence of GABABR vs GABAAR responses likely reflects differential sensitivities of GABAARs and GABABRs.
source: This difference in prevalence likely reflects differential sensitivities of GABAARs and GABABRs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the difference in prevalence.

claim: Activation of GABAARs on UBCs requires high GABA levels.
source: Activation of GABAARs on UBCs requires high GABA levels (Möhler, 2006), and thus requires a direct PC synapse for effective activation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Activation of GABAARs on UBCs requires a direct PC synapse for effective activation.
source: Activation of GABAARs on UBCs requires high GABA levels (Möhler, 2006), and thus requires a direct PC synapse for effective activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high GABA requirement.

claim: GABABRs are activated by much lower levels of GABA than GABAARs.
source: GABABRs are activated by much lower levels of GABA (Galvez et al., 2000; Kaupmann et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A direct PC input is not required for GABABR activation on UBCs.
source: Consequently, a direct PC input is not required and GABA released from PC synapses onto neighboring cells can pool and spillover to activate GABABRs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low GABA requirement for GABABR activation.

claim: GABA released from PC synapses onto neighboring cells can pool and spillover to activate GABABRs on UBCs.
source: Consequently, a direct PC input is not required and GABA released from PC synapses onto neighboring cells can pool and spillover to activate GABABRs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low GABA requirement for GABABR activation.

claim: The combined activity of many PCs could efficiently activate GABABRs on UBCs and control spontaneous activity.
source: This also suggests that the combined activity of many PCs could efficiently activate GABABRs on UBCs and control spontaneous activity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism of GABABR activation.

claim: Both UBCs and PC collaterals are present throughout the cerebellar cortex, albeit at a lower density than in lobule X.
source: It is important to note that we have focused on PC feedback to UBCs in lobule X. Both UBCs and PC collaterals are also present throughout the cerebellar cortex, albeit at a lower density.
evidence: This is based on the anatomical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: It remains to be seen whether PC to UBC feedback occurs in other regions besides lobule X.
source: It remains to be seen whether PC to UBC feedback occurs in other regions, and if it does, whether it has the same target dependence.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the study.

claim: The failure rate and potency of the fast component of inhibition are similar for PC synapses onto UBCs and granule cells.
source: The failure rate and potency of the fast component of inhibition are similar for PC synapses onto UBCs and GrCs (Guo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work cited.

claim: The overall effect of fast and stochastic GABAAR PC inhibition of UBCs and granule cells is to lower the gain of the input layer.
source: Therefore, we hypothesize that the overall effect of fast and stochastic GABAAR PC inhibition of UBCs and GrCs is to lower the gain of the input layer.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the functional role of fast PC inhibition.

claim: PCs slowly inhibit granule cells primarily by activating special high-affinity α6 and δ subunit-containing GABAARs.
source: PCs slowly inhibit GrCs primarily by activating special high-affinity α6 and δ subunit-containing GABAARs that are specialized to respond to low levels of extracellular GABA (Brickley et al., 1996; Hamann et al., 2002; Kaneda et al., 1995; Wall and Usowicz, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: α6 and δ subunit-containing GABAARs are specialized to respond to low levels of extracellular GABA.
source: PCs slowly inhibit GrCs primarily by activating special high-affinity α6 and δ subunit-containing GABAARs that are specialized to respond to low levels of extracellular GABA (Brickley et al., 1996; Hamann et al., 2002; Kaneda et al., 1995; Wall and Usowicz, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: α6/δ containing GABAARs in granule cells and GABABRs in UBCs can both respond to low GABA levels that reflect population-averaged PC firing rates.
source: It appears that α6/δ containing GABAARs in GrCs and GABABRs in UBCs can both respond to the low GABA levels that reflect the population-averaged PC firing rates, and in both cases, the kinetics of the responses are slow (312 ms in GrCs vs. 580 ms in UBCs).
evidence: This is a comparison of the properties of slow inhibition in GrCs and UBCs.

claim: The kinetics of slow PC inhibition are similar in granule cells (312 ms) and UBCs (580 ms).
source: It appears that α6/δ containing GABAARs in GrCs and GABABRs in UBCs can both respond to the low GABA levels that reflect the population-averaged PC firing rates, and in both cases, the kinetics of the responses are slow (312 ms in GrCs vs. 580 ms in UBCs).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of kinetics.

claim: The major differences between slow PC inhibition of UBCs and granule cells are the state change that can occur in UBCs and the target dependence of the UBC inhibition.
source: The major differences between slow PC inhibition of UBCs and GrCs are the state change that can occur in UBCs, and the target dependence of the UBC inhibition, neither of which have been described for PC inhibition of GrCs (Guo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison highlighting differences between PC inhibition of UBCs and GrCs.

claim: State changes and target dependence have not been described for PC inhibition of granule cells.
source: The major differences between slow PC inhibition of UBCs and GrCs are the state change that can occur in UBCs, and the target dependence of the UBC inhibition, neither of which have been described for PC inhibition of GrCs (Guo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on comparison to prior work cited.

claim: Increases in PC firing lead to slow increases in inhibition of UBCs.
source: Increases in PC firing lead to slow increases in inhibition, and following decreases in PC firing rate this inhibition gradually decreases.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data showing graded GABABR responses.

claim: Following decreases in PC firing rate, inhibition of UBCs gradually decreases.
source: Increases in PC firing lead to slow increases in inhibition, and following decreases in PC firing rate this inhibition gradually decreases.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data showing graded GABABR responses.

claim: PC firing may be able to alter UBC-mediated transformations in the input layer of the cerebellum.
source: We conclude that PC firing may be able to alter UBC-mediated transformations in the input layer of the cerebellum.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Slow inhibition could allow PCs to dynamically regulate the excitability of mGluR1+ UBCs.
source: Slow inhibition could also allow PCs to dynamically regulate the excitability of mGluR1+ UBCs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional role of slow inhibition.

claim: Mossy fiber inputs to the cerebellum can modulate the firing of Purkinje cells.
source: MF inputs to the cerebellum can modulate the firing of PCs, and these firing rate changes will feedback to mGluR1+ UBCs to alter their firing.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar circuitry.

claim: PC firing rate changes will feedback to mGluR1+ UBCs to alter their firing.
source: MF inputs to the cerebellum can modulate the firing of PCs, and these firing rate changes will feedback to mGluR1+ UBCs to alter their firing.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequences of the PC to UBC feedback circuit.

claim: PC feedback to UBCs could be particularly important for UBCs that fire for more than 10 s in response to a brief mossy fiber activation in the absence of inhibition.
source: This could be particularly important for UBCs that fire for more than 10 s in response to a brief MF activation in the absence of inhibition (Guo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on prior work cited.
